subject: system-design
title: Abstractions in System Design
summary: Why we design with components that hide their internals behind a simple contract — and what happens when that contract leaks.

blocks.text: An abstraction hides how something works behind a simple contract. You use it through its interface — what it promises to do — without knowing the machinery underneath. A load balancer 'spreads traffic across servers'; you rely on that promise without tracking which server each request lands on.

A large system has more moving parts than any one person can hold in their head. Abstractions let you reason about it one layer at a time: trust each component's contract, and think about how the contracts fit together rather than how every part is built.

items: They contain complexity — a database's contract is 'store and query data', not its B-trees and write-ahead log.
They make parts swappable — anything honoring the contract can be substituted, so you can change the implementation without touching callers.
They give a shared vocabulary — 'put a cache in front of it' means the same thing to everyone on the team.

blocks.text: Most of system design is composing a handful of well-understood building blocks — load balancers, caches, queues, databases, object stores. Each is an abstraction with a known contract and known tradeoffs, so a design becomes a conversation about which blocks to use and how to wire them, not a from-scratch invention.
This is why the building blocks are worth learning once, deeply: every system design reuses the same pieces in a new arrangement.

The contract is a simplification, and reality occasionally pokes through. A remote call looks like a local function call — until the network is slow, drops the request, or the other side is down. Treating a leaky abstraction as if it were perfect is where many outages begin.

blocks.title: Know what leaks
blocks.text: Use abstractions to think, but stay aware of what each one hides — latency, failure, and cost are the details that leak through most often.
So design with building blocks for their clarity, but keep their tradeoffs in view. The skill is choosing the right abstraction and knowing exactly where its contract stops holding.
